newsitem.title: BELGIUM: RENAULT GUILLOTINE FOR BELGIAN PLANT SHOCKS NATION.
newsitem.headline: RENAULT GUILLOTINE FOR BELGIAN PLANT SHOCKS NATION.

text.p: A decision by French car maker Renault to stop production in Belgium is a kick in the teeth of the whole country, Belgian commentators said on Friday.
"Guillotine for Renault Volvoorde," said a banner headline in daily De Morgen. "'New industrial strategy' kills Belgian plant," financial daily De Financieel-Economische Tijd said.
Renault said late on Thursday it would close its assembly plant at Vilvoorde, near Brussels, in July with a loss of 3,100 jobs as part of a wider reorganisation of production.

As Renault workers blockaded the doomed factory, holding finished cars hostage, newspapers held out little hope the decision would be reversed, focusing instead on possible implications for the whole of Belgium's car assembly business.
There were also xenophobic tones in the editorials.

"Renault is still half state-owned and it prefers to close factories outside France's borders. That is old fashioned and unjust. But it is unlikely that the Renault bosses will change their minds," De Standaard newspaper said in an editorial.
It noted Renault was the smallest assembler in Belgium, behind Ford , Opel , Volkswagen and Volvo.

"Renault gives the whole Belgian car industry a slap," Gazet Van Antwerpen said in a headline. It quoted Opel Belgium boss Leo Valvekens as saying he had not seen the Renault closure coming and there were no plans for Opel to follow suit.
Le Soir said that with 1,275,534 cars assembled in 1995, Belgium was ahead of Germany, France and Japan in terms of production per head of population.
"The latent question is: what is the future for the other four assembly plants in Belgium? The question of the quality of the Belgian workforce is no longer a sufficient argument," Le Soir said.
Political reactions were not slow in coming, focusing on the suddenness and harshness of the decision.

Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, who lives in Vilvoorde and visited the plant for an awards ceremony just last weekend, said in a statement he was dismayed by the "brutal and unilateral decision of the French management of Renault."

"Renault Vilvoorde risks becoming a victim of a strategic decision... which takes no account of the social repercussions on the area," he said, calling on the Flemish regional government to seek ways to find other industrial uses for the area and thus preserve jobs.
Renault is looking for another car maker to take over the plant, but a Renault spokeswoman said no talks had started.
